blocks.text: 过去一年，我们与全球一些最大型企业中的数十万名开发者合作。在与这些团队并肩工作的过程中，我们构建并不断打磨了一套前沿的智能体运行框架（agent harness），直接满足企业开发的需求：在复杂任务上给出高质量结果、高效利用资源，并具备强大的安全管控。

inlines.text: 过去一年，我们与全球一些最大型企业中的数十万名开发者合作。在与这些团队并肩工作的过程中，我们构建并不断打磨了一套前沿的智能体运行框架（agent harness），直接满足企业开发的需求：在复杂任务上给出高质量结果、高效利用资源，并具备强大的安全管控。

blocks.text: 今天，我们推出 Droid 1.0：它比以往更准确、更高效、也更快，背后是全新的设计原则和一套程序化工具调用引擎。

inlines.text: 今天，我们推出 Droid 1.0：它比以往更准确、更高效、也更快，背后是全新的设计原则和一套程序化工具调用引擎。

blocks.text: Droid 是我们的智能体运行框架。所谓运行框架，指的是模型之外的一切：提示词、工具、工具结果的返回方式，以及驱动这一切运转的循环。如今智能体可以连续工作数小时甚至数天、跨越数百个回合，而每个回合都要重新发送指令、工具和历史记录。

blocks.text: 程序化工具调用

inlines.text: 程序化工具调用

blocks.text: 在标准的智能体循环中，模型直接调用工具，每次工具输出都会追加到上下文中。程序化工具调用（PTC）则针对长周期任务采取了不同的思路：智能体编写一个程序来调用这些工具。

inlines.text: 在标准的智能体循环中，模型直接调用工具，每次工具输出都会追加到上下文中。程序化工具调用（PTC）则针对长周期任务采取了不同的思路：智能体编写一个程序来调用这些工具。

blocks.text: 借助 PTC，智能体可以先进行推理，为工具调用工作流编写代码，然后在一次调用中端到端执行整个程序。例如，它可以编写一个工作流来读取数百个文件并找出其中提到某个主题的少数几个，对数十个 Linear 工单进行分诊，或者按照确定性流程分步执行一次棘手的数据库迁移。

blocks.text: 我们在 Droid 1.0 中将 PTC 设为默认，原因有三。第一，它能让智能体的上下文窗口保持干净，因为它收到的只是其程序的输出。普通的工具输出（原始文件、搜索结果、日志）作为变量留在程序内部。第二，它减少了模型请求次数，因为一个程序可以运行多次调用，从而让复杂任务更快、更便宜。第三，它让智能体更可靠：检查和循环在代码中确定性地运行，消除了模型可能偷懒、尽管原本计划过却漏掉某个情况的可能性。

因 harness 之外的原因失败的试验会重跑：评测未能启动、模型请求超时，或提供商容量不足。
Anthropic 的内容审核在 Claude Opus 5.5 上拦截了部分任务。对每个遇到此情况的 harness，这些试验都在 Claude Opus 5 上重跑，直到不再出现内容审核错误。GPT 模型没有此类拦截。

blocks.text: Programmatic tool calling

inlines.text: Programmatic tool calling

blocks.text: In a standard agent loop, the model calls tools directly and every tool output is appended to its context. Programmatic tool calling (PTC) takes a different approach to long-horizon work: the agent writes a program that invokes the tools.

inlines.text: In a standard agent loop, the model calls tools directly and every tool output is appended to its context. Programmatic tool calling (PTC) takes a different approach to long-horizon work: the agent writes a program that invokes the tools.

blocks.text: With PTC, the agent can reason up front, write the code for a tool-calling workflow, and then execute the entire program end to end in a single invocation. For example, it could write a workflow to read hundreds of files and find the few that mention a topic, triage dozens of Linear tickets, or run a tricky database migration in pieces following a deterministic process.

blocks.text: CodeAct (Wang et al., 2024) showed that acting through code beats JSON and text tool calls across 17 models. Cloudflare and Anthropic brought the idea to production in late 2025, and Codex brought it to coding agents this year.

blocks.text: We made PTC the default in Droid 1.0 for three reasons. First, it keeps the agent's context window clean, because all it receives is the output of its program. Ordinary tool outputs (raw files, search results, logs) stay inside the program as variables. Second, it cuts the number of model requests, because one program runs many calls, which makes complex tasks faster and cheaper. Third, it makes the agent more reliable: checks and loops run deterministically in code, eliminating the chance that a model could be lazy and drop a case despite originally planning it.

Calls that don't depend on each other run concurrently, so a batch takes as long as its slowest call.

blocks.text: The loop starts when a model first becomes accessible, often as an early-access snapshot. Every proposal is held to the same principles:
Budget every token, and keep large tool results in files.
Grow the request by always maintaining the prompt cache.
Profile the hot path to inference, and cache anything you can.
Track background work, such as long commands and subagents, and wake the model when it finishes.
When the agent gets stuck, always have a next step ready: nudge, retry, summarize, or stop.

No single change moved every model, but together the three met the goal on all of them.

blocks.text: Bounded autonomy

inlines.text: Bounded autonomy

blocks.text: The longer an agent runs on its own, the more ways it can get stuck, repeat work, or drop the task entirely. Droid detects each of these, and every case results in a defined next step: a nudge, a retry, or a stop. The rules live in the loop rather than the model, so they hold for every provider Droid supports, and a new model gets them on day 0.

blocks.text: Getting stuck usually shows up in the stream. On Factory-managed Anthropic streams, 4 minutes of silence counts as a dropped stream and is retried. A response that hits a hard time limit gets at most two attempts, and one that breaks partway through is removed before the retry, so the model builds only on complete answers.

blocks.text: With requests cached and trimmed, the model's response time was mostly out of our hands. How quickly we got the request to it was not. Droid rebuilt its list of connected apps on every turn, and pre-flight tool lookups slowed down as session histories grew.

blocks.text: The first turn had the most overhead. Sign-in checks duplicated work and ran one after another. Startup requests waited for all of Droid's code to load, and the first model request waited for every MCP server to settle. Users bringing their own Amazon Bedrock credentials faced an additional delay while those credentials loaded.

blocks.text: In our latest update, each of those waits is gone or out of the way. Droid reuses its list of connected apps until a connection changes, cutting turn preparation to 24 ms. In a controlled test, that change alone made the median response finish 13% sooner. Droid now reads only the newest part of the session history, so pre-flight tool lookups take about a millisecond. Sign-in checks run in parallel without repeats, dropping from 101 ms to 59 ms median. droid exec sends its identity, feature-flag, org-policy, and connector requests together while its code is still loading, cutting median time to the first model request from 1,741 to 646 ms. MCP servers start alongside the first turn, so a server that takes 3 seconds to initialize no longer holds it up, and Bedrock credentials are ready before the first request. Beyond the user's machine, a routing fix in our inference proxy shaved 150 ms off every model call.

blocks.text: Opening is the first wait in every session. Between the August 25 and October 20 releases, median time to first paint fell from 1,839 to 488 ms, and time until Droid accepted a prompt fell from 1,876 to 618 ms, cuts of roughly 70% each. Most of that came from doing less before the first frame. Droid now ships precompiled code, so about 6,000 modules are no longer parsed at launch. Keystrokes register while startup finishes, and CI fails any change that pushes first-keystroke p95 above 250 ms. Upgrading to Bun 1.4.2 cut p95 startup time by 13–22% across Linux, macOS, and Windows, and for the last, Droid now also skips console setup and caches the system certificate list.

blocks.text: Methodology

inlines.text: Methodology
Head-to-head.
Versions used:
claude-code@2.1.306
cursor-cli@2026.10.19-6bbf2c4
opencode@2.1.2
Models used: Claude Opus 5.5 (high reasoning) and GPT-6.1 Sol (high reasoning).
High reasoning was chosen as it is the most popular reasoning option on our platform, thus best representing the workloads delegated to Droid.
Benchmark: Terminal-Bench 4, all tasks, default time limits, run October 23–28, 2026.
Each harness ran three trials per task.
Trials that failed for reasons outside the harness were rerun: the eval failed to launch, a model request timed out, or the provider was out of capacity.

Anthropic's content moderation stopped some tasks on Claude Opus 5.5. For every harness that experienced this, those trials were rerun on Claude Opus 5 until no content moderation errors occurred. GPT models had no such blocks.

Devin has no way to turn off its tool for asking the user a question, so on some tasks using GPT-6.1 Sol it stopped to ask instead of finishing. To keep the comparison fair, a task where Devin stopped to ask was counted as passed if Codex passed it (an average of 4.7 tasks per trial). This affects accuracy only, not cost or time.
Cursor undercounts tokens when it reconnects mid-task, so for the two trials this occurred in we estimated the missing usage from the transcript.
Cost and time are per passed task, at each provider's list price. Charts run cost from most expensive on the left to cheapest on the right.
Droid is compared with one harness at a time, on the same model.
We only count tasks that both harnesses passed in all three trials, so both are measured on the same work.
Cost is based on tokens used, priced at list price.
Time is how long the agent spent working, not counting setup or grading.
Everything else.
Every change described here runs in production Droid.
Production numbers come from Droid's own telemetry, with CI excluded: prompt reuse, launch medians for the newest release each week, quit times, and the first-turn trace.

Prompt reuse is measured per request: the share of input tokens read from the provider's cache, over 20.4M production Droid CLI requests in the 7 days to Oct 22, with CI and evals excluded. Weighted by tokens instead of by request, the share is 91.5%. Append-only is the share of requests the prompt-cache monitor did not flag.
Some metrics related to startup time come from controlled tests that compare the builds before and after a change on the same tasks and machine.
Modeled numbers are the direct-call side of the Script examples: 10 calls per request at the low end, 3 at the high end, and about 28,000 tokens of fixed instructions per request.
